Subject: Comments on Request for Information to Inform Interagency Working Group on 
Mining Regulations, Laws, and Permitting, Docket No. DOI-2022-0003-0001 
 
To whom it may concern: 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide input to the Interagency Working Group on Mining 
Regulations, Laws, and Permitting. Wildsight is a leading conservation organization working in 
British Columbia's Columbia Basin. Our mission is to work locally, regionally, and globally to 
protect biodiversity and encourage sustainable development.  
 
Wildsight has been a leader in land-based conservation for decades and is actively engaged in 
British Columbia’s efforts to modernize B.C.’s mining laws and the Canadian Federal 
government's proposed Coal Mining Effluent Regulations. Wildsight, along with our network of 
colleagues within Canada and the U.S., are currently working towards a solution to the ongoing 
selenium contamination crisis in the transboundary Elk-Kootenay(i) Watershed originating from 
four operating open-pit coal mines in the Elk Valley. We believe Wildsight is uniquely 
positioned to provide the Interagency Working Group with valuable perspectives on Canada’s 
and B.C.’s mining laws.  
 
Although B.C. prides itself on being a world-class mining jurisdiction, fundamental changes 
need to occur to B.C.’s mining laws to protect taxpayers from financial liabilities, uphold 
Indigenous Rights, and protect the environment. This doesn’t go without realizing mistakes made 
within B.C. and Canada, along with efforts to modernize mining laws, can inform better policy 
decisions in other jurisdictions.  
 
 

 
1) Limiting the extent of mining in transboundary watersheds 
 
Significant pollution concerns exist1,2 along the Taku, Stikine, Unuk-Nass, and Elk-Kootenay(i) 
watersheds, where polluted waters cross the Canada-U.S. border. The most impactful step the 
Biden Administration can take in protecting the environment and creating a path forward to 
modernizing Federal mining laws is by referring each of these watersheds to the International 
Joint Commission. The International Joint Commission was formed to prevent and resolve 
disputes over shared waters between Canada and the U.S. As Canada and the U.S. look to 
further partner in the development of critical minerals, the establishment of watershed boards 
under the International Joint Commission to review projects that affect the water flowing 
across the border will ensure communities and the environment are protected. 
 
2) Protect communities and the environment from toxic mine waste  
 
On August 4th, 2014, a tailings storage facility collapsed releasing an estimated 25 million cubic 
metres of wastewater and tailings at the Mount Polly copper and gold mine in south-central 
B.C. Mine tailings dams pose a significant risk to local communities and the environment. The 
Safety First: Guidelines for Responsible Mine Tailings Management3 should be used to help 
inform and create new regulations surrounding the construction and maintenance of mine 
tailings and mine waste storage facilities. The Safety First: Guidelines for Responsible Mine 
Tailings Management was developed in 2020 by an international group of 142 scientists, 
community groups, and NGOs from 24 countries. 
 
3) Institute a polluter pays principle with robust financial assurances and full reclamation 
bonding 
 
There are approximately 500,000 abandoned mines that will require reclamation within the 
U.S., and in B.C., an estimated 10% of active mines will require perpetual wastewater 
treatment. The Britannia mine located in B.C.'s Sea to Sky Corridor required $46 million in 
public funds to control acid rock drainage, with an additional annual cost of $3 million for water 
treatment. Coal mines within B.C.'s Elk Valley will likely require substantially more funding to 
stem selenium contamination.  
 
The BC Mining Law Reform4 Closure, Reclamation & Abandoned Mines report5 highlights 
needed policy changes that can protect the environment and communities while ensuring mine 
reclamation occurs. Some of these recommendations include requiring companies to provide 
full security for independently reviewed reclamation costs before permitting, the establishment 
of emergency funding that can cover the costs to reclaim abandoned mines sites and mining-
related disasters that active mining companies can contribute to proportionally, and requiring 
mining companies to cover the costs of reclamation before paying creditors in cases of 
bankruptcy. 
 
 

 
4) Free, prior, and informed consent of Indigenous Peoples 
 
The Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (Declaration Act)6 was a positive step 
taken by B.C. to establish the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples7 
as the province’s framework for reconciliation. Furthermore, the existing claim system needs to 
be modernized to ensure Indigenous rights, land use planning, communities, environmental 
protection, and private property are not undermined. 
 
In summary, efforts to drastically modernize outdated federal hardrock mining regulations, 
laws, and the permitting process such that communities and the environment are protected are 
desperately needed. Policy work completed by groups like the BC Mining Law Reform Network 
(see Summary Reccommendations8), as well as learning from past mistakes like those outlined 
within the 2016 Auditor General of British Columbia: An Audit of Compliance and Enforcement 
of Mining Sector9, can help to guide better policy. Although B.C. is known as a world-class 
mining jurisdiction, it has failed to uphold its international commitments under the Boundary 
Waters Treaty to prevent mine-polluted waters from crossing the Canada-U.S. border. New U.S. 
mining policy needs to carefully consider the risks associated with mining in transboundary 
watersheds and should consider making these mining-free areas. Mining should not 
compromise the multiple uses of public lands, especially considering mine reclamation typically 
cannot restore previous levels of biodiversity, and in some cases leads to further abandoned or 
toxic sites that no one can use. Adopting similar legislation like Canada’s Federal Impact 
Assessment Act10 or British Columbia's Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act6 and 
referring to the Summary Recommendations8 by the BC Mining Law Reform Network will 
improve the U.S.’s current outdated mining laws and go a long way in protecting communities 
and the environment from the negative mining impacts. 
 
 
Sincerely  
 
 
 
 
 
 
Wyatt Petryshen, M.Sc. 
Mining Policy and Impacts Researcher, Wildsight 
wyatt@wildsight.ca

Dear Sirs:  
The Uranium Producers of America (UPA) is a national trade association representing the 
domestic uranium mining and conversion industries. UPA members conduct uranium 
exploration, development, and mining operations in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska, New Mexico, 
South Dakota, Texas, Utah, and Wyoming. UPA members operate valuable, high-grade uranium 
deposits that provide good, high-paying jobs, tax revenues, and produce clean energy for the 
citizens of the United States. UPA’s mission is to promote the viability of the nation’s uranium 
industry, while being good stewards of the environment in which we work and live. 
UPA commends the Department of the Interior for seeking pertinent input from 
stakeholders on whether existing laws and regulations need to be changed and if, after reviewing 
input from the Request for Information (RFI), changes are warranted, how to implement those 
changes. This is especially important given the Administration’s position that domestic minerals, 
such as uranium, are to be incentivized in order to meet the Administration’s climate, emissions 
reductions, and clean energy goals. It is without question that nuclear-generated electricity must

RFI Question 1: Eliminating Mining Claims and Substituting a Leasing System. 
Would alternatives to the existing claim system, such as leasing, or 
adjustments to the current system, such as incorporating mining 
into comprehensive federal lands use assessments and planning, 
lead to better outcomes for communities, the environment, and a 
secure domestic supply of minerals? If so, how should such an 
alternative or adjusted system be structured? 
Given the elusive nature of mineral deposits, uranium discoveries cannot occur without 
widespread exploration. Such extensive exploration activities are required because 
concentrations of useful minerals rich enough to form economic ore deposits are rare 
phenomena. Finding new resources and delineating their economic potential is critical to keeping 
the uranium pipeline flowing. The Mining Law governs land tenure and authorizes citizens to 
obtain mineral rights on certain public lands. The current mining claim system gives claim 
owners the required security of land tenure to support the large investments necessary to explore 
for uranium and develop mines. Changing to a leasing system would eliminate land tenure 
security, significantly reduce already declining uranium exploration and development on public 
lands, thus further increasing U.S. reliance on foreign minerals, such as the uranium presently 
imported from Russia and its allies. 
 
1 See “Stats show that closing Indian Point was a ‘mistake’ for New York,” Nuclear Newswire, July 29, 2022.

The Biden Administration has an ambitious goal of reducing U.S. greenhouse gas 
admissions by more than 50 percent from 2005 levels by 2030.2 Included in this effort is a goal 
of producing 100 percent of U.S. electricity from carbon-free sources by 2035. Converting from 
a life-of-mine claims system to a time-limited lease would substantially interfere with the 
Administration’s policies to increase domestic uranium production in order to strengthen the 
domestic nuclear fuel supply chain and provide the domestic uranium industry required to 
support clean energy. 
The U.S. leasing system is designed for large, already-defined mineral deposits. This 
system is unworkable for scarce and difficult to locate uranium deposits. The 1872 Mining Law 
creates the tenure needed for operators to make the substantial investments of time, knowledge, 
and money to explore for uranium with the hope of discovering an economical deposit to 
develop into a mine. The self-initiation process leverages private-sector investment to encourage 
mining operations that create jobs, pay taxes, and provide fuel for the nation’s largest carbon-free 
supply of electricity. All of this is accomplished at no risk or expense to the U.S. taxpayer.  
Furthermore, experience shows that prior limited transitions of individual minerals to 
mineral leasing from the mining claims system have created years of delay and legal uncertainty. 
For example, the Mineral Leasing Act of 1920 converted oil shale from a locatable mineral to a 
leasable mineral. Despite the Act’s clear intention to protect valid existing claims, the 
Department of Interior instead spent decades invalidating oil shale mining claims grandfathered 
by the Mineral Leasing Act. Not until the Energy Policy Act of 1992 was this issue finally 
resolved. With the Administration’s efforts to decarbonize our energy supply and the targeted

2030 reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, now is not the time to replace the current mining 
claims system. 
The Department of Energy experimented with a uranium leasing program in Colorado. 
This program attracted little interest and has produced no development of any operations. The 
program did not encourage mining. 
The public benefits from private-sector investment in uranium exploration and 
development projects using the current mining claims system and would not achieve better 
outcomes by substituting a leasing system. 
RFI Question 2: 
Are there international mining best practices or standards that the 
United States should consider adopting, or encouraging the U.S. 
mining industry to adopt? If so, which practices or standards and 
what improvements or benefits would they provide? 
The legal framework and guidelines governing the responsible development of uranium 
resources in the U.S. are more comprehensive and rigorously tested than in any other uranium 
producing country in the world.  
Today’s domestic uranium operations must comply with federal and state environmental 
laws and regulations. Surface and water management and reclamation laws are in place to direct 
uranium exploration and mining operations. Uranium miners must reclaim their operations when 
mining is complete according to a plan put in place before operations can commence. Further, 
operators must provide state and federal regulators with pre-approved reclamation bonds and 
other forms of financial assurance to guarantee the operation will be properly reclaimed. The 
financial assurance is calculated based on what it would cost the regulatory agency to reclaim the 

U.S. Department of Interior 
RFI: Working Group on Mining Regulations, Laws, and Permitting 
August 30, 2022 
Page 5 
 
mine should the operator fail to do so. The assurance can also provide for long-term 
maintenance, if necessary.  
In 2018, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) issued a final rulemaking for 
Section 108(b) of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act 
(CERCLA) that held EPA did not need to develop a separate financial assurance program for the 
minerals industry. EPA found the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM), the U.S. Forest 
Service’s (USFS) and state’s existing environmental regulations and financial assurance 
programs effectively protect the environment at modern mining operations and guarantee that 
taxpayers will not have to pay to reclaim mines. EPA concluded the environmental laws and 
regulations enacted since the late 1960’s have had an enormous positive impact in changing how 
modern mines operate. 
RFI Question 3: 
If the U.S. were to place royalties on hard rock minerals produced 
from public domain lands, what factors should be considered and 
what structures would best protect the interests of the taxpayer 
while responsibly incentivizing production? 
In addition, if royalties were collected, how should those revenues 
be allocated? 
In April 2020, the Nuclear Fuel Working Group (NFWG) reported that the domestic 
mining and conversion industries are at the most immediate risk due to our over-reliance on 
imported uranium. The NFWG warned against reliance on unfriendly state-owned enterprises 
(SOE’s) using their uranium production for geopolitical advantages to our country’s detriment.3 
The SOE’s manipulate their currency, do not comply with strict environmental standards, and

practice price suppression. Adding any type of additional royalties for uranium concentrates 
produced on federal lands would only exacerbate the SOE’s unfair advantages. 
The Department of Energy and Department of Defense have recognized the critical 
importance of a strong domestic fuel cycle. DOE officials have briefed key Congressional 
committees on a multi-billion dollar effort to revitalize the front end of the nuclear fuel cycle. 
Domestic uranium production is a key component of this plan. Given this effort, it is not time to 
provide additional roadblocks, such as royalties, to revitalize the domestic uranium industry. To 
impose a royalty on uranium produced on public lands at this time would have a devastating 
impact on our nation’s ability to produce this critical material for the carbon-free electricity 
necessary to meet the Administration’s decarbonization goals. The domestic production industry 
is essentially dormant due to the price-cutting and non-competitive practices by Russia and its 
SOE partners as evidenced by the Department of Commerce’s report on its investigation of the 
industry’s 232 petition. Adding additional royalties, particularly a gross royalty, would 
needlessly increase the already non-level playing field for U.S. producers attempting to compete 
against SOE’s who do not have a profit requirement. 
For many years, the mining industry has explained why a gross royalty structure like that 
on the oil and gas industry is unworkable and unfair. Using coal, oil, and gas royalty programs as 
a template for a uranium royalty is ill-conceived and impractical because of the substantially 
different geological characteristics of these minerals compared to uranium. Oil, gas, and coal are 
easier to find than uranium, requiring less exploration time and investment. Uranium must also 
undergo expensive processing steps to produce a saleable product.

RFI Question 4:  
What changes to financial assurance requirements for mining 
should be considered? 
As noted in UPA’s response to RFI question 2, this issue was thoroughly reviewed by 
EPA in 2018. EPA concluded that existing programs under the federal land management 
agencies’ surface management regulations (e.g. BLM’s 43 CFR Part 3809 regulations and USFS’ 
36 CFR Subpart 228 regulations) provide comprehensive protection and financial assurance: 
EPA has determined that modern regulation of hard rock mining 
facilities … reduces the risk of federally financed response actions 
to a low level such that no additional financial responsibility 
requirements for this industry are appropriate.4 
RFI Question 5:  
How might the U.S. best support reclamation of existing AML 
sites including the development of meaningful good Samaritan 
proposals as well as remining and reprocessing of mine tailings 
and waste, where feasible? 
Currently any funds more than what BLM requires to administer mining claims goes to 
the Department of Treasury’s general fund. These excess funds should be directed to Abandoned 
Mine Lands (AML) reclamation. According to BLM’s 2020 Public Lands Statistics Report, this 
would provide approximately $30 million for AML reclamation.5 
In addition, Clean Water Act and Superfund liability issues should be addressed to allow 
for third-party Good Samaritan AML reclamation projects. S. 3571, “The Good Samaritan 
Remediation of Abandoned Hardrock Mines Act of 2022” has the potential to provide direction 
to address the liability issues at AML sites that do not have complex water quality issues.

Good Samaritan legislation has been studied and endorsed by NRC/NAS and the Western 
Governors’ Association. It is time for Congress to eliminate the liability exposure that prevents 
new mining operators with no previous involvement with an abandoned mine from undertaking 
voluntary reclamation activities. 
The Administration’s 100-day report includes evaluating the reprocessing of mine wastes 
as a viable source of critical minerals. Mine wastes at abandoned mines should be included in 
this evaluation. To encourage reprocessing and reclamation of AML sites containing critical 
mineral resources, new operator re-mining and reprocessing proposals should be exempted from 
the Clean Water Act and CERCLA liability so long as the new operator’s proposal demonstrates 
operations in compliance with current regulatory standards. 
RFI Question 6:  
What would a successful mine reclamation program include? Are 
there existing programs that the U.S. should adopt? 
As noted in UPA’s response to RFI question 4, the EPA’s 2018 conclusions regarding the 
scope and success of existing reclamation programs and requirements have answered this 
question. Compliance with BLM’s 43 CFR Subpart 3809 and USFS’s 36 CFR Subpart A 
regulations ensure that mineral exploration and mining operations on public lands will be 
successfully reclaimed. To enhance our uranium supply chain and cut off reliance on Russian 
uranium, the current system should not be changed. 
Successful mine reclamation has been accomplished in Wyoming following Chapter 11 
of the Wyoming Non-Coal rules. The DOI should look at these rules as a workable example.

RFI Question 7:  
How can Tribes and local communities be effectively engaged 
early in the process to ensure that they have meaningful input into 
the development of mine proposals? 
Uranium deposits and cultivation operations are frequently located in close proximity to 
tribal lands and communities and as such, uranium operators make a concerted effort to work 
collaboratively and productively with tribes. Uranium operators rely on members of these 
communities to fill the jobs created by the projects and recognize that this will require training 
and a safe working environment to attract the qualified workforce necessary for a project’s 
success. Educating the local community and Tribal members as to the advances in mining 
methods and technologies is a key aspect in ensuring these stakeholders have the knowledge and 
understanding to provide meaningful input into the development of mine proposals. The existing 
requirements under the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) and National Environmental 
Policy Act (NEPA) provide notice and public opportunities for comment and consultation in the 
permitting process. 
Tribes and local communities are intimately involved in licensing decisions, and 
regulators actively seek their input. The existing requirements under the National Historic 
Preservation Act (NHPA) and NEPA provide notice and public opportunities for comment and 
consultation in the permitting process. 
As a concrete example of active engagement, a UPA member, Energy Fuels, is in active 
discussions with its White Mesa Mill neighbor, the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, to determine how 
best to alleviate the Tribe’s project concerns. The company cooperates closely with state, federal 
and Tribal sponsored studies to assess potential environmental or health impacts from its 

U.S. Department of Interior 
RFI: Working Group on Mining Regulations, Laws, and Permitting 
August 30, 2022 
Page 10 
 
operations. The Ute Mountain Ute Tribe recently announced that they will be conducting a 
health impact study for the White Mesa Mill and Energy Fuels expects to participate in the study. 
Energy Fuels has been a long-time supporter of STEM education programs for Native 
American high school students (the Fields program) and it provides scholarships annually to 
local students. In addition, the producer created the San Juan County Clean Energy Foundation 
to support local education, health/wellness, environmental and Tribal communities. The 
company seeded the Foundation with a one million dollar contribution and has committed to 
contribute 1% of top-line revenues from the White Mesa Mill to the Foundation each year. An 
initial contribution from the Foundation is currently planned for a Native American education 
initiative. 
Finally, Energy Fuels actively seeks out local Naïve Americans for its work force and 
about 50% of its current employees at the White Mesa Mill are Native American. These workers’ 
average salaries are well above the San Juan County average. 
Another example of benefits to underserved communities from uranium operations can 
be found with enCore Energy’s south Texas ISR operations. EnCore leases land principally from 
small private land owners whose families have held their land since the days of the Spanish land 
grants in Texas. Those leases provide lease bonuses, annual rentals, and ultimately royalties to 
these families. This allows them to realize revenue from their land to support their families in 
two of the poorest counties in Texas. Eighty percent of these land owners are Hispanic and are 
local to the area in which enCore operates. The revenue allows these families to hold onto their 
land rather than lose it to tax sales or forced sales to large corporate land companies and ranches.

The Texas counties in which enCore operates have suffered losses of jobs and 
populations as the primary energy businesses centered on oil and gas have moved away as the 
country migrates to less fossil fuel demand under the Administration’s clean energy plan. 
EnCore’s uranium operations, in the past, have been the largest, single non-governmental 
employer in these counties. As enCore advances toward restarting production, it will create 
nearly one hundred jobs that have starting wages that are more than double the local minimum 
wage. EnCore has strong support from the local communities and the county governments who 
see its operations as a way to transition from their economy being overly reliant on oil and gas 
operations toward producing fuel for clean energy in the form of nuclear power. 
EnCore’s operations sustain these local communities by hiring a local workforce and 
supporting local businesses in underserved communities. A Brooks County Judge told enCore’s 
executives that every dollar it spends locally turns hands seven times across many local 
businesses, improving the local economy, lifestyles and services. EnCore’s operational 
improvements provide property tax revenue that supports the local schools in these communities. 
In addition to the example of how enCore’s operations support underserved communities 
in Texas, the company also has assumed leases on New Mexico Spanish Land Grant properties 
in New Mexico. In addition to lease rentals and advance royalty payments that support the Land 
Grants’ operation budgets over the past 12 years, enCore and its predecessors have provided 
nearly one million dollars in scholarship funds that have supported youth from the Land Grants’ 
families in pursuit of higher education.

August 30, 2022

The examples of these two uranium companies are followed by other producers. The 
operators create positive impacts through employment, local purchasing, taxes, scholarship 
programs and other community participation in rural communities throughout the southwest. 
Regulatory authorities could enhance Tribal involvement by improving the NHPA 
process by creating specific guidance to navigate this process so all parties are aware at the 
outset of the goals of the consultation process. 
RFI Question 8:  
How could updates to the Mining Law of 1872, or other relevant 
statutes, help provide more certainty and timeliness in the 
permitting process? 
The difficulty and time it takes to permit an operation on public lands is a major deterrent 
to incentivize domestic uranium production. The ten- to fifteen-year period it often takes to 
permit a project adds investment-deterring uncertainties for mine operators and their investors. 
Unnecessary administrative and legal delays do not improve environmental stewardship, but they 
do harm the rural communities that must wait years for the jobs, tax revenues and other 
socioeconomic benefits mining operations provide.  
To facilitate and expedite the responsible domestic production of uranium and other 
critical minerals, the permitting process must be streamlined. This can be done without 
sacrificing the “hard look” required by the NEPA process. Excessive NEPA appeals and 
litigation create these delays and uncertainties. NEPA can unfortunately be manipulated to use 
appeals and litigation to purposely create lengthy and costly project delays that have little or 
nothing to do with the merits of a case. 

U.S. Department of Interior 
RFI: Working Group on Mining Regulations, Laws, and Permitting 
August 30, 2022 
Page 13 
 
To address the permitting log jam, NEPA, or its implementing regulations, should be 
amended to establish reasonable timelines for agency action. Once the mining industry has 
provided the necessary baseline and site characteristics for a project, the reviewing agency 
should act promptly in reviewing the potential environmental impacts and hold comments to 
reasonable but specified timelines. Changes to improve the practicality of the NEPA analysis 
process, the readability of NEPA documents and better agency coordination should be put into 
regulation.  
Congress has recently evaluated ways to improve the permitting process in the 
Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. These include: 
1. Establishing and adhering to timelines and schedules; 
2. Engaging in early cooperation among agencies, project sponsors and affected 
stakeholders, including state, local and Tribal governments; and 
3. Provide demonstrable improvements in the performance of federal permitting and 
review processes, including lower costs and more timely decisions.  
In summary, curbing unnecessary litigation delays and uncertainty that does nothing to 
further environmental stewardship would help create more certainty for operators already 
struggling to remain competitive globally with state-owned entities abroad that are not subject to 
the same economic pressures or as vigilant in measures protecting health, safety, and the 
environment.  
RFI Question 9:  
What improvements can be made to the mine permitting process 
without reducing opportunities for public input or limiting the 
comprehensiveness of environmental reviews? 
The Interagency Working Group can take direction from Section 40206 of the 
Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to improve the mineral permitting process. The 

U.S. Department of Interior 
RFI: Working Group on Mining Regulations, Laws, and Permitting 
August 30, 2022 
Page 14 
 
streamlining measures in Section 40206 could provide a template for Mining Law updates to 
provide more certainty and timeliness to the permitting process. Specific ways to improve the 
quality and timeliness of federal permitting and review processes include: 
(1) 
establishing and adhering to timelines and schedules for the consideration of, and 
final decisions regarding applications, operating plans, leases, licenses, permits, 
and other use authorizations for critical mineral-related activities on federal land; 
(2) 
establishing clear, quantifiable, and temporal permitting performance goals and 
tracking progress against those goals; 
(3) 
engaging in early collaboration among agencies, project sponsors, and affected 
stakeholders –  
(a) 
to incorporate and address the interests of those parties; and 
(b) 
to minimize delays; 
(4) 
ensuring transparency and accountability by using cost-effective information 
technology to collect and disseminate information regarding individual projects 
and agency performance; 
(5) 
engaging in early and active consultation with state, local, and Tribal 
governments –  
(a) 
to avoid conflicts or duplication of effort; 
(b) 
to resolve concerns; and 
(c) 
to allow for concurrent, rather than sequential, reviews; 
(6)  
providing demonstrable improvements in the performance of federal permitting 
and review processes, including lower costs and more timely decisions; 
(7) 
expanding and institutionalizing federal permitting and review process 
improvements that have proven effective; · 
(8) 
developing mechanisms to better communicate priorities and resolve disputes 
among agencies at the national, regional, state, and local levels; and

Dear Mr. Feldgus, 
 
The State of Idaho appreciates the opportunity to summit comments in response to the Request for 
Information to Inform Interagency Working Group on Mining Regulations, Laws, and Permitting. On 
February 22, 2022, the Interior Department announced the formation of an Interagency Working Group 
(IWG) on reforming hardrock mining laws, regulations and permitting policies. On March 31, 2022, the 
Interior Department published a Request for Information in the Federal Register seeking information on 
the proposed reform. The Idaho Department of Lands (IDL) offers a perspective on mining in Idaho and 
some comments in response to the Request for Information.   
 
Mining is an important part of the Idaho economy. From the famed Silver Valley in northern Idaho to the 
fertile phosphate mines of southeast Idaho, the value of total nonfuel mineral production for 2021 in 
Idaho was $722 million as reported by the United States Geological Survey. Billions of dollars in mineral 
processing and product manufacturing infrastructure rely on a steady supply of ore from mines in Idaho.  
 
Idaho is strongly supportive of any effort to cut red tape and streamline permitting. Idaho state employees 
work closely with our federal counterparts at the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and U.S. Forest 
Service (USFS) to review and administer mining plans of operation. The interagency review process 
works well, but Idaho has seen too many mineral projects struggle through environmental review and 
permitting process that take 10-years or more. The U.S. and Idaho have some of the strongest 
environmental requirements in the world, and Idaho believes that environmentally sustainable mining is 
critical to the mining industry. However, efficient environmental review and permitting do not need to 
come at the expense of strong environmental protections.  
 
Below are comments and suggestion on the proposed interagency mining reform: 
 
Align the USFS 228 regulations with the BLM 3809 regulations  
Having one set of standards on these federal lands would be helpful for operators and cooperating 
agencies during National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) reviews. In some cases, the BLM regulations 
should be kept; for example, the BLM allows the use of trust funds that can generate meaningful revenue, 
while the USFS does not. In other instances, the USFS regulations should be kept if they make more 

  
sense. The two sets of regulations are very similar already, but a few differences exist, and these 
differences cause confusion and may not add much protection to the taxpayers and our federal lands. 
 
Eliminating mining claims is not needed and provides an unnecessary disruption to the current mining 
framework 
Mining claims provide a security of tenure needed for operators. Exploration is often expensive and time 
consuming. Patenting provisions in the current mining law have had a moratorium for over 20 years, and 
patenting seems to be the biggest point of contention with regard to mining claims. We suggest removing 
the ability to patent mining claims and let the free market adjust accordingly.  
 
International Mining Best Practices and Improvement of Permitting 
The Department of Interior should explore the permitting practices of other Western countries that 
maintain high environmental standards, such as Australia and Canada. The U.S. often takes 10-12 years to 
permit new mining projects, whereas Australia and Canada can process permits in approximately two 
years while maintaining environmental standards that are on par with the U.S. Australia and Canada 
employ several practices in their mineral permitting that could reduce permitting times in the U.S. 
 
Permitting delays can have negatives impacts across industries. Long permitting processes and 
unexpected permit requirements increase project costs on mining companies and make them riskier 
investments. Delays and long permitting processes also create ripples down the supply chain and industry 
creating uncertainty throughout the economy. 
 
Some Australian states, for example, have an integrated permitting authority that can issue many or all 
relevant environmental permits for a single project. The Department should consider efficiencies that 
could be possible with a centralized National Environmental Policy Act office that could perform 
environmental reviews for large projects and provide a centralized source of information and decision-
making. 
 
In Canada and Australia, the applicant is responsible for completing the environmental study and 
submitting it to state and federal permitting agencies. In the U.S., applicants are currently allowed to fund 
the environmental analysis that is conducted by a federal agency. The Department should explore the 
benefits of allowing applicants to perform the environmental analysis and submit it to agencies for 
approval, and what safeguards would be necessary to ensure it is objective and fact-based. 
 
Canadian provinces schedule the review process, roles and responsibilities of each agency, and target 
dates for completion of each stage at the beginning of application period. Federal assessment of whether 
the project is likely to cause significant harm to the environment occurs within 365 days. The only 
completion dates that are not determined in the schedule are those that apply to submission by the 
applicant, placing responsibility for any delays on the applicant rather than the permitting agencies.  
 
The Department should also consider increasing resources and expertise available to mineral permitting 
offices. Agencies are often understaffed and lack sufficient expertise to efficiency evaluate environmental 
analysis and reviewing permits.  
 
If a leasing framework is needed for mining on federal lands, then a leasing and royalty system similar 
to what the states have for their trust lands may work better than the proposed 12.5%royalty rate.  
Royalties for specific commodities may vary depending on whether they have a global market price or a 
more locally driven price. The revenue derived from leasing should be directed to state and federal 
agencies for abandoned mine lands reclamation.  
 
 
 

  
Changes to Financial Assurance 
Federal land management agencies should have the ability to hold financial assurance bonds for 
reclamation. The Miscellaneous Receipts Act has proven to be a barrier for the U.S. Forest Service. 
Federal agencies should also have flexibility in how bonds are invested and given access to a wider range 
of investment vehicles. The Department should also consider regulations that allow states to hold 
financial assurance bonds while ensuring they will not be held legally liable under the Comprehensive 
Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA) or any other federal laws. 
 
Good Samaritan legislation is a must  
State agencies need access to a program like CERCLA that allows for cleanup of sites that pose human 
health/environmental hazards while not requiring full compliance with water quality standards. Many of 
these sites are on private lands in remote areas with no power supply and no year-round access, which 
precludes costly water treatment systems. Waste consolidation and incremental improvements to water 
quality can still be achieved at these sites without the threat of litigation under the Clean Water Act and 
CERCLA, but only if state agencies have the protection of Good Samaritan legislation.  
 
Long term AML funding for physical hazards and human health/environmental hazards is needed 
Especially for non-energy commodities.  
 
Early Local and Tribal Engagement 
Engagement at the earliest possible stages of a project is critical to building community support and 
reducing administrative and legal challenges later in the process. Applicants and land management 
agencies should be required to engage with a host of local stakeholders prior to the scoping period.  
 
Stakeholders should include, but not be limited to: Native American Tribes; state and local governments, 
environmental justice groups; labor organization; industry; and non-governmental organizations and 
environmental, recreation, and conservation groups. The Department should also consider revising its 
public notice procedures beyond the Federal Register and local newspapers and make a proactive effort to 
reach members of the local community in a wider range of mediums. 
 
Reforms to the 1872 Mining Law 
Changes to the mining law will not create any addition certainty and timeliness to the environmental 
review or permitting processes, which are governed by other laws and regulations such as the Mining and 
Mineral Policy Act of 1970 and the National Materials and Minerals Policy, Research and Development 
Act of 1980 and federal regulations. NEPA is the largest obstacle to timely permitting, and Idaho is 
pleased to see the Administration undertaking NEPA reform. Idaho encourages the Administration to 
address aspects of NEPA that create permitting and environmental review delays. 
 
Agency expertise to provide in-depth review of mining plans is needed  
With staff attrition through retirements there has been a loss of engineering and mining expertise in the 
federal government. Modernized regulatory standards are an excellent goal. Effective implementation of 
these standards relies on experienced staff.  
 
Incentives for Critical Mineral Development 
Developing the U.S.’s domestic supply of critical minerals is an urgent task if the U.S. is to meet the 
Biden Administration’s goal of a decarbonized economy by 2050 and stave off the worst impacts of 
climate change. Idaho has a vast supply of minerals currently on the critical mineral list, such as cobalt, 
antimony, tantalum, arsenic, niobium, fluorspar, tungsten, vanadium, zirconium, and hafnium. The World 
Bank Group has estimated that demand for critical minerals will increase by 500% by 2050.  
 
The Department should consider streamlining NEPA review for critical mineral projects or establishing 
an expedited process for mineral listed on the U.S. Geologic Survey’s Final List of Critical Minerals. 

  
The Department should increase funding the U.S. Geological Survey’s Critical Minerals Mapping 
Initiative to map critical mineral deposits across the U.S. to create a transparent map for mineral 
companies to reference as they consider exploring for critical mineral supplies. 
 
The Department should also regularly review its critical minerals list to be able to add and remove certain 
minerals as their status changes. The Department should also consider adding phosphate to the critical 
minerals list. 
 
Continued cooperation with state agencies is needed 
When federal agencies preempt state authority it complicates the regulatory framework for operators and 
the public.  
 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide these comments. Some additional discussion between the IWG 
sub-groups and affected states is recommended in order to better focus and implement the proposed 
changes.

thousands of projects reviewed pursuant to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).  We 
undertook these studies to better understand the NEPA process, the frequency of and risks 
associated with NEPA litigation, and to identify factors associated with projects experiencing 
lengthy reviews.  We believe that our empirical studies play a valuable role in designing NEPA 
reform because of the information they provide, and because our research paints a picture that 
departs from commonly held assumptions about NEPA.  The stories that make for the best 
headlines are rarely representative of common agency practice.  We also believe that our 
observations about NEPA practices apply more broadly to other federal permitting processes and 
can inform efforts to build a resilient supply chain.  
 
Our most recent research reviewed over 41,000 U.S. Forest Service (USFS) projects that 
underwent NEPA review.6  Our analysis considered the year of project initiation, the geographic 
region where the project occurred, the interaction between up to 43 different activities involved 
in each project, and the level of analysis undertaken for each project.  Despite spending months 
developing a complex multivariate regression model to identify factors associated with project 
delays, we were successful in predicting only twenty-five percent of the variance on NEPA 
review completion times.  Twenty percent of the variance was attributed to one variable alone—
the level of analysis.  This result makes sense.  Projects subjected to the searching review of an 
Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) were likely to take longer than projects that underwent 
only the most basic review required by a Categorical Exclusion.  Notwithstanding this 
predictable result, we also observed that level of analysis alone did not dictate completion times.  
The fastest 25% of EISs were completed more quickly than the slowest 25% of Environmental 
Assessments (EAs), which require a less exhaustive analysis.  Similarly, the fastest 25% of EAs 
were completed more quickly than the slowest 25% of CEs, which require only a very limited 
environmental analysis.  This overlap suggests that factors other than the regulatory requirements 
of NEPA influence completion times.  It also demonstrates that the NEPA review process can be 
completed quickly and efficiently, even at the most rigorous level of review.  Thus, eliminating 
analytical rigor is not necessary to achieve efficient decision-making. 
 
Our research revealed that most NEPA projects are completed within a predictable 
timeframe, though significant outliers are not uncommon.  There are multiple and overlapping 
explanations for delay.  One explanation that should not be overlooked is that the NEPA review 
process is indeed working as designed, identifying potential issues that would have otherwise 
escaped consideration and driving a reassessment of options and impacts before an irretrievable 
commitment of resources occurs.  Slower projects may reflect iterative changes to improve the

proposed action or minimize impacts.  This possibility reminds us that NEPA’s goal is to make 
better decisions, not faster decisions. 
 
A report from the Government Accountability Office (GAO) studying hardrock mine 
permit processing times supports this explanation.7  Between 2010 and 2014, the Bureau of Land 
Management and the Forest Service approved 68 mine plans of operations.  The majority (55%) 
were processed in less than 18 months, and 63% were processed in under two years.8  This 
appears to indicate that permit applications can be processed efficiently.  The remaining 37% 
were spread out over a wide timeframe, with six applications taking longer than four years.   
 
The GAO identified 13 causes of delay and the amount of time associated with each 
factor.  Some explanations for lengthy delays included: (1) incomplete or unacceptably vague 
permit applications (identified as a problem by 91% of BLM and Forest Service respondents); 
(2) changes in mine plans that substantially increased the size of the proposed mine or relocated 
boundaries after the mine plan had been submitted (identified as a problem by 70% of BLM and 
Forest Service respondents); and (3) efforts to mitigate complex and consequential 
environmental problems (identified as a problem by 65% of BLM and Forest Service 
respondents), like impacts to water quality.9   
 
From the GAO report, it appears that it is not uncommon for permit applicants to 
substantially increase the size or scope of the proposed mine or to relocate the proposed mine 
boundaries, roads, and other facilities after the mine plans had been submitted and the agency 
had started the review process.  Changing mine plans can add months to mine plan reviews, 
depending on whether the changes require officials to supplement fieldwork to include areas not 
contained in the original proposal, or require resource specialists to revise completed analyses 
and reports.10  Delays such as these are not attributable to federal permitting processes and 
cannot be avoided by streamlining the permitting process.  Updating analysis to reflect new 
information and changed conditions, moreover, is consistent with agency regulatory 
obligations.11 
 
In our empirical analysis of Forest Service decisions, we also observed that a less 
rigorous level of analysis often fails to deliver faster decisions.  In other words, reducing 
environmental analysis does not automatically result in faster decisions.  Delays were often 
attributable to factors external to the NEPA review process.  Inadequate agency budgets, staff 
turnover, delays receiving information from permit applicants, and compliance with other laws 
were some of the primary causes of delay identified in our research.  These observations comport 
with the GAO’s findings, which noted that “limited resources allocated to the field office, such as 
number of staff, staff expertise, funding, infrastructure, training, and/or computer technology” 
was the second most common reason for permitting delays (behind only incomplete and vague 
permit submissions), impacting 28% of mine permitting efforts.12

In the sections below, we focus on ways to expedite mine permit processing by 
expanding agency capacity.  In our research, we observed that agency capacity includes three 
elements: (1) staff availability; (2) professional confidence to make difficult decisions that may 
be litigated; and (3) expertise and institutional knowledge.  In Section B, we discuss ways to 
avoid delays caused by insufficient agency capacity and litigation aversion.  In Section C, we 
discuss ways to build agency capacity by facilitating regulatory expertise and expanding 
institutional knowledge.    
B. Avoiding Delay Caused by Insufficient Agency Capacity and Litigation Aversion. 
 
One persistent and overarching cause of delay involves insufficient or inconsistent staff 
availability.  Not only are agencies chronically understaffed, agencies also are frequently forced 
to temporarily reassign staff in response to changing agency priorities.  Nowhere was this better 
illustrated than with the Forest Service, which frequently reassigns staff in response to 
wildfires.13  These reassignments, while unavoidable in many ways, result in project delays and a 
lack of continuity between team members.  The lesson is clear—agencies must have sufficient, 
adequately trained, and stable staffing if they are to complete any permitting task in a timely and 
efficient manner.   
 
The GAO made a similar finding regarding hardrock mine permitting in a report issued in 
2016.14  The second most common source of delay was insufficient agency staff in certain critical 
positions, which caused a bottleneck in NEPA review process and increased the length of time to 
review the plan.15  The GAO’s findings are consistent with a report issued by the National 
Research Council seventeen years earlier.16  “Staff shortages are likely to be at least partially 
responsible for the excessive delays experienced in NEPA reviews and issuance of permits.”17  
The National Research Council went on to note, “Some land management offices report that they 
have too few people to conduct inspections, review proposed operating plans, process appeals, 
and conduct other required activities.  This concern extends beyond the numbers of people. . . . 
Offices responsible for regulating mining projects may not always have access to the trained and 
experienced personnel required.”18  In other words, there are two distinct elements to agency 
capacity: (1) staff availability and (2) expertise or institutional knowledge. Both elements affect 
permitting times. In order to improve permitting efficiency without compromising environmental 
protection, agencies must have both elements—sufficient staff and the necessary expertise.  
 
The longstanding problem of agency capacity has been exacerbated in recent years.  
Between 2016 and 2020, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) reported losing almost 300

not guarantee that agencies are making good or informed decisions.”30

procedural laws like those noted above by failing to take a hard look at all aspects of a proposed 
action.  A study of twenty years of Forest Service Land Management litigation revealed that in 
the pool of cases decided on the merits, more than half of the time (67%), the Forest Service 
would have lost even if NEPA did not exist.31  In other words, truncating thoughtful 
consideration of a project and exploration of alternatives during the NEPA process may create or 
exacerbate delays caused by litigation.

C.  Reducing Delay Caused by the Complexity of the Legal and Regulatory 
Structure by Facilitating Regulatory Expertise and Expanding Institutional 
Knowledge. 
 
Another significant source of delay involves navigating the intricate and complex array of 
laws applying to mining operations.  Simply figuring out what law applies, how to apply the 
regulatory standard, and who has authority to issue the relevant permits can be a daunting task 
for both agency officials and permit applicants.  Regarding the regulatory structure of hardrock 
mine permitting, the National Research Council observed,  
[T]he complexity of various programs can make the system difficult to 
understand, approach, and implement efficiently.  As a result, mining regulation, 
permitting, monitoring, reclamation, closure, and post-closure becomes a series of 
negotiations carried on against a background of regulatory requirements and 
programs.  This means that governmental regulators at all levels need a significant 
degree of sophistication and training in order to make these programs efficient and 
effective.  The programs do not—and cannot—operate in cookbook fashion.32 
 
In other words, implementing a complex regulatory structure requires institutional 
knowledge and expertise.  New agency staff do not have the same experience as the senior staff 
members they are replacing.  Additionally, without senior staff on hand, new agency officials 
will not have the benefit of mentoring, guidance, or instruction.  As a result, the “sophistication 
and training” necessary to make the mine permitting program efficient and effective is at risk.  
This loss of institutional memory will affect permit processing times and may reduce the 
effectiveness of the agency to negotiate environmental protections against the backdrop of 
regulatory requirements.   
 
Uncertainty about how the permitting process works, the standard to apply, and who is 
responsible for making a decision causes two types of delay.  First, conducting research to 
confirm the permitting process with each application adds time and creates inefficiencies in the 
preparation and review of each application. Second, hard problems without obvious answers tend 
to sit on the back of the desk, especially when there is a fear of repercussion for making the 
wrong decision.  Reducing procedural and legal uncertainty within this complex labyrinth will 
improve efficiency and assist both regulators and applicants. 
1. The legal and regulatory structure for hard rock mining is complex, multi-
faceted, and lacks uniformity.  Without clear guidance, this legal structure 
causes delay. 
 
The current legal and regulatory structure varies by mineral category, surface/subsurface 
estate ownership, and with the agency owning or entity charged with managing surface and 
subsurface resources.33  In general, minerals fall within three categories: saleable, leasable, and 
locatable (hard rock).  Each category has different statutory frameworks and regulatory

The difference between locatable and leasable minerals has consequences for land use 
management.  The Federal Land Policy Management Act (FLPMA) guides the BLM’s 
management of lands that are subject to both mineral leases and claims as well as nearby public 
lands that may be necessary to access or develop minerals.  Management requirements are 
imposed through its land use planning requirements, and subject to the duty to administer public 
lands on the basis of multiple use and sustained yield.45  Similarly, the National Forest 
Management Act informs the Forest Service’s surface management of lands that are subject to 
mineral leases and claims as well as lands that must be crossed to access and develop minerals.46  
In contrast, mining operations for locatable minerals are primarily governed by the General 
Mining Law of 1872.  Land management plans developed pursuant to FLPMA and the National 
Forest Management Act may directly and severely restrict a mining claimant’s ability to access 
newly staked claims, conduct exploration phase activities on those claims, and to use adjacent 
lands for other mining related purposes.  New management plan requirements are, however, 
likely to have less impact on existing claims.  With a few exceptions, such as lands that have 
been withdrawn47 and Wilderness Study Areas, the BLM’s authority to regulate surface 
management of locatable mineral operations derives primarily from its authority to prevent 
unnecessary or undue degradation of public lands.48   
 
Once a claim or lease has been obtained, access to the minerals secured, and exploration 
has demonstrated the viability of the operation, the miner will still need to obtain mining plan 
approval and as well as numerous other environmental and land use approvals.  Many states 
exercise delegated statutory authority over aspects of mine permitting.49  Some federal statutes, 
like the Clean Water Act, contain provisions allowing the federal agency to delegate its 
permitting authority to the State.  In addition to these federal statutes, state or local laws may 
also impose additional permitting requirements, including state environmental review 
requirements, like the California Environmental Quality Act.  When reviewing the hardrock 
mining permit application process, the Government Accountability Office identified six 
categories of federal permits and authorizations and seven categories of state and local permits or 
authorizations that mine operators may need to obtain from entities other than the BLM and the 
Forest Service.50

2. Create a Mine Permitting Hub with flowcharts and environmental checklists to 
make the legal Structure more transparent, predictable, and manageable.

expedite the permitting process would be to create a public, geographically-organized database

II. 
Land Use Planning as a Tool to Expedite Mine Permitting. 
 
Mining on federal public lands involves compliance with land management laws and 
regulations that operate independent of the General Mining Law.  For simplicity, our comments 
focus primarily on the BLM’s surface use management authority.  The BLM manages more land 
and resources than any other federal agency, with responsibility for over one-tenth of the total 
surface area of the United States and almost one-third of all minerals.73  The BLM, like the 
Forest Service, is statutorily charged with managing lands under its care in accordance with  
multiple use and sustained yield principles, unless lands are set aside for another purpose.74  The 
National Forest Management Act shares many of FLPMA’s features, and the logic of comments 
analyzing FLPMA and its implementing regulations can also extend to the Forest Service’s 
management authority and regulations.75   
 
The process for determining which federal public lands should be open to mineral claim 
and development, and the land use standards that should apply to those lands, are complex and 
multifaceted, reflecting the myriad values at stake as well as the BLM and USFS’s broad and 
sometimes conflicting statutory mandates.  Planning and permitting laws can be used to 
streamline critical mineral development without compromising environmental protection, 
transparency, or public and intergovernmental engagement.  
 
Assessing the existence of a mineral deposit within a planning area, the potential for 
mineral development, and the level of certainty associated with mineral information is a critical 
component of the BLM’s resource inventory process.76  This information supports subsequent 
land management plan development.   
 
Land management laws and regulations can be used to create an expedited permitting 
path for critical mineral developments that meet rigorous environmental and good governance 
goals.  This approach relies on a suite of incentives and disincentives developed pursuant to 
existing federal land management laws.  These incentives do not require legislation and can be 
accomplished with relatively minor regulatory changes.  We discuss some possible approaches 
below.  As noted earlier, expediting the permitting process through proactive land management 
decisions depends on sufficient agency capacity to conduct the planning process and complete 
the requisite analysis.  Thus, the recommendations below must work in concert with the 
recommendation to increase agency budgets, staff, and expertise. 
 
BLM and Forest Service land management plans incorporate closures to future mineral 
claim entry that are required by other laws, such as the Wilderness Act.  Management plans also 
reflect mineral withdrawals imposed by executive action, such as national monuments designated 
by a President pursuant to the Antiquities Act.  The BLM and USFS may also, in certain 
circumstances, withdraw public lands from availability for future mineral claim entry.77  Such

BLM managed lands are governed by land use stipulations contained in the applicable 
land and resource management plans, subject to valid existing rights.  Land use stipulations are 
applied to protect sensitive areas and the resources those areas contain. For example, an area may 
be identified as an important aquifer recharge area; an area rich in cultural or archaeological 
resources; as critical breeding, rearing, foraging, or refugia for high valued wildlife species; as a 
highly valued visual landscape; or based on a host of other possible important values that may 
exist in isolation or overlap with one another.   
 
Stipulations may, for example, close a sensitive area to all surface disturbing activity.  
Such a stipulation may be appropriate where, for example, activity on a steep and erosive slope 
would cause an unacceptable risk of landslides or sediment delivery to a stream or lake.  A no 
surface occupancy stipulation could also be used to protect critical wildlife habitat or cultural 
resources.  These types of measures may be necessary to achieve the BLM’s multiple use and 
sustained yield mission or to avoid unnecessary or undue degradation.78  A surface closure, 
however, does not necessarily close an area to subsurface development.  Oil and natural gas 
resources underlying areas subject to a surface closure may still be accessed and developed using 
directional drilling technologies if surface facilities are located outside of the closure area.  
Building on such an approach, a mining company could theoretically conduct underground 
mining or solution mining beneath an area subject to a surface closure if surface uses associated 
with mining operations were located outside of the area subject to the no surface occupancy 
stipulation, were technically and economically feasible, and that the operation complied with all 
other applicable laws, regulations, and land use stipulations.  
 
Federal land managers may also conclude that adequate resource protection could occur 
without closing an area to all surface development.  The BLM or USFS may, for example, 
require that surface uses meet strict visual quality standards to minimize use conflicts, or be 
subject to seasonal restrictions to minimize wildlife conflicts or address soil plasticity.  In some 
instances, it may be impossible to fully develop the land surface under these stipulations, or 
development may become prohibitively expensive.  While strict surface use stipulations may 
preclude certain types of mine operations, such as surface mining, they may still allow 
underground mining or solution mining to occur.  
 
Still other areas are subject to normal surface use terms and conditions because these 
areas can be developed without causing unacceptable impacts, or where impacts are deemed 
acceptable in light of competing resource values and uses.   
 
Where a mining interest has staked a valid mining claim and that claim preceded 
development of land use stipulations contained in the applicable land and resource management 
plan, the mining interest generally retains the legal right to mine even if subsequent land use 
designations would otherwise preclude mining.  The right to access and mine minerals that is 
available under such valid existing rights, however, is subject to reasonable regulation as needed 
to protect competing resources and land uses.  Land management stipulations that apply to

A. Opportunities to use the land-use planning process as a tool to identify landscape-
specific general performance standards, landscape-scale mitigation opportunities, 
and to avoid unnecessary or undue degradation. 
 
There may be some critical mineral deposits that cannot be accessed without degrading 
other values, such as watersheds, drinking water, fish stocks, and human safety.  In these cases, 
the BLM should recognize its statutory obligation to avoid unnecessary and undue degradation 
of public lands.79  BLM’s mining regulations incorporate stipulations contained in land use plans 
as general performance standards.80  General performance standards may also include mitigation 
measures identified by the BLM.81  Thus, all mining operations—whether conducted under a 
notice or a plan of operations—are required to comply with the applicable BLM land use plans, 
activity plans, and coastal management plans, as appropriate.  Compliance with the general 
performance standards is required to avoid unnecessary or undue degradation while conducting 
operations on public lands.82

opportunities to minimize or offset unavoidable impacts.  The BLM’s Mitigation Manual, 
authorizes the BLM to use the land use planning process to identify resources that are 
“important, scarce, sensitive, or have a protective legal mandate” and to identify mitigation 
standards for those resources.83  Using the mitigation hierarchy, (avoid, minimize, and

B. 
Opportunities to improve planning and permitting using the NEPA process. 
The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) applies to major federal actions that are 
likely to impact the environment.  While NEPA does not mandate elimination or avoidance of 
environmental impacts, it does require disclosure and analysis of alternative means of achieving 
project goals, the impacts that are likely to result from implementation of each of these 
alternatives, and opportunities to mitigate impacts.  This analysis must precede issuance of a 
federal permit or authorization.  NEPA’s disclosure and analysis requirements thus facilitate 
informed decisionmaking and public engagement.  NEPA also appears to provide a mechanism 
to coordinate compliance with multiple environmental laws, thereby leading to faster permit 
completion.91  There are two ways in which the NEPA process could be used to expedite 
permitting: (1) initiating a programmatic EIS to identify resource conflicts, define general 
performance standards, and identify mitigation measures likely to be associated with resource 
conditions; and (2) using the NEPA process to facilitate and promote coordination among 
permitting authorities. 
1. Using a Programmatic EIS to analyze cross-cutting environmental issues and 
prioritize areas for avoidance. 
 
Although the analysis required by NEPA is most often applied at the site or project level, 
NEPA can also be used programmatically.  Programmatic Environmental Impact Statements 
(PEISs) have been used successfully to identify areas that are appropriate for renewable energy 
development, accelerating subsequent analyses and permitting.  The Department of the Interior 
(DOI) was able to create positive screens to expedite solar energy development across a six-state 
region by identifying factors such as solar exposure and aspect, and access to the electrical grid.  
Using this information, the DOI compared these positive screens against screens identifying 
resource constraints, like critical habitat for threatened and endangered species and culturally 
important landscapes.  The DOI then used this comparison to identify areas possessing high 
resource potential that avoided major resource conflicts.92  A similar programmatic effort was 
used to facilitate wind development across an eleven-state region.93  These programmatic 
analyses enabled the BLM to direct development toward those areas.  
 
While we support efforts to programmatically identify priority areas for renewable energy 
development, we believe that it would be difficult to complete a similar programmatic EIS to 
identify priority areas for strategic mineral development.  First, there are fifty different minerals 
on the DOI’s list of critical minerals.  Information about deposits of these minerals and what 
development of each deposit would involve is less readily accessible or uniform than information 
about solar exposure or wind speed.  Developing a base of information sufficient to identify 
priority development areas for each mineral would be an expensive and time-consuming task.

Done properly, the NEPA process functions as an umbrella statute, facilitating 
compliance with a host of other laws such as the Clean Water Act, the National Forest 
Management Act, or the National Historic Preservation Act.  Indeed, permitting decisions that 
undergo NEPA review are often completed faster than those that are exempted from NEPA.106  
We believe this may reflect the interagency coordination that is part of the NEPA process as well 
as improvements in efficiency that come with improved communication and coordination.  
 
Delays are likely to increase where interagency coordination is lacking.107  As the 
National Research Council observed, “Timing of environmental review and permitting is 
affected by agencies’ ability to coordinate with one another, as well as by the availability of 
sufficient agency staff and technical resources.  Where coordination among state and federal 
regulatory agencies is high, environmental review and permitting appears to be faster . . . where 
separate agencies engage in serial permitting, rather than coordinating their review efforts, the 
process-including data gathering—can take longer.”108  
 
Early consultation is essential to ensure coordination.109  Early consultation should 
include all stakeholders including the relevant federal, state, and county agencies, tribes, citizen 
groups, and the applicant.110  NEPA’s analytical process can provide a structure for ensuring that 
a proposed plan of operation “complies with all pertinent Federal and state laws.”111  NEPA’s 
scoping process could be used to identify all relevant state, federal, and local permits that would 
be necessary, as well as the individual officer responsible for approving or denying a permit.  
Because the statutory and regulatory regime governing hard rock mining is so complex, simply 
identifying the applicable legal standards and the responsible official would bring clarity for all 
regulatory authorities, the public, and the permittee.  The scoping process could also define the 
sequence of permitting, and appropriate timelines for permitting decisions within that sequence.  
This approach, which has been successfully used for transportation projects, would significantly 
reduce delays caused by ambiguity, confusion, and reluctance to act.112   
Proactively requiring all stakeholders to engage in NEPA’s scoping process can expedite 
permitting by identifying issues of contention early and clarifying information that must be 
gathered.  “Agreement might not be reached among all of the stakeholders.  However, the issues 
would be better understood by the public and defined to the benefit of the public, the agencies, 
and the applicant if early consultation occurred under NEPA and permitting process.”113

Including all stakeholders at the beginning of the NEPA process also provides an 
opportunity to initiate consultation requirements early.115  This approach would provide three 
benefits.  First, engaging in consultation early maximizes the opportunity to avoid problems at

In summary, the NEPA process can be used to expedite mineral development in two 
ways.  First the BLM could initiate inter-agency programmatic analyses of cross-cutting 
environmental issues.  This would avoid repetitive and duplicative review at the site level.  It 
would also make the permitting process more predictable and transparent by identifying resource 
conflict areas, clarifying performance standards, and articulating principles that will guide 
application of the mitigation hierarchy.  Second, at the site level, the NEPA process can be used 
to coordinate permitting requirements and improve communication between permitting officials 
at the federal state, tribal, and local level.  The NEPA process can also be used to initiate 
consultation requirements early in enough in the process to be meaningful and effective, which 
can avoid delays in the long run.  These procedures can improve timeliness, predictability, and 
transparency in the permitting process.  Achieving these outcomes, however, depends upon 
sufficient agency capacity and expertise to utilize these tools effectively.
